rules.questionText: The 'question' string is given to both arms byte for byte, with no other words.
rules.keyFacts: Grade text claims against the key facts that apply to the configuration the explainer shows. 'core' facts count for coverage and clarity. A claim that contradicts an applicable key fact is an error. 'appliesTo' is 'all', 'conventional' or accepted-variant ids. 'acceptedWordings' lists accepted wordings and limits and is shown to graders. 'designerNote' and 'factCheck' are provenance and are never shown to graders.
rules.mechanismChecks: Five checks per question (M1 parts, M2 connections, M3 direction, M4 ratio or timing, M5 geometry). RUBRIC.md defines PASS, FAIL, NOT SHOWN, N/A and (for M3 and M4 only) CANNOT JUDGE. A clause about an invisible quantity is NOT SHOWN unless readable values or calibrated graphics show it.

checkLabels.verified-web: A web source seen on 2026-11-11 states the fact. The textbook citation names the standard reference by chapter topic; the designer did not re-read the book for this pre-registration.
checkLabels.textbook-only: A standard textbook fact. The designer's web check did not find a source page. Pending until the fact-check gate.
checkLabels.derived: Follows by arithmetic from constants or other key facts, as the note shows.
checkLabels.single-source: Only one inspected source supports the whole fact (fact check, 2026-11-11).
checkLabels.fact-check-only: Added from a fact-check report's description of an accepted variant; no web source was inspected for it. Core: false.

rules.graderView: Graders never see this file. They see GRADER-QUESTIONS.json, made from it by tools/grader_questions.py: the question id and text, each key fact's id, fact, core flag and acceptedVariants, and the mechanism checks. No category, sources, check labels, designer notes, nearShipped notes or anything about how outputs are made.
rules.configurations: Each question names its 'conventional' configuration and its 'acceptedVariants' (other physically correct configurations). The question text does not change. If an explainer shows a correctly explained accepted variant, a fact or a check clause that does not apply to it is N/A (RUBRIC.md).

questions.question: How does a compound gear train get a big speed reduction from small gears?
questions.teachingValue: Shows why stage ratios multiply and why a compound shaft carries two gears; the basis of clocks, gearboxes and winches.

keyFacts.fact: For a fixed-axis mesh, speed out / speed in = driving teeth / driven teeth (in magnitude). The driven gear turns slower only if it has more teeth. An external mesh reverses the direction of rotation.

A compound train has at least one shaft that carries two or more gears fixed to turn together at the same speed. Their tooth counts are usually different, chosen to give the stage ratios, but they need not be.

In a fixed-axis compound train, the stage speed ratios multiply. As a train value, speed out / speed in = product of driving teeth / product of driven teeth: two 12-to-36 stages give 12/36 x 12/36 = 1/9. As a reduction ratio, speed in / speed out = product of driven teeth / product of driving teeth: 36/12 x 36/12 = 9:1. Both conventions are correct.
acceptedWordings: Train value 1/9 and reduction ratio 9:1 are both correct; a grader must not count either convention as an error.
keyFacts.designerNote: Norton (6th ed.), section 9.8, defines the compound train and derives the multiplied stage ratios (read by the Sol fact check). The Omni two-gear calculator no longer counts as a source.

keyFacts.fact: Each external mesh reverses the direction of rotation. With two external meshes the output turns the same way as the input. An idler gear changes the direction but not the ratio.

In steady operation, power out = efficiency x power in, and torque out / torque in = efficiency x speed in / speed out. A reduction increases the available torque after losses; it does not create power.
Gears that mesh must have the same tooth size (module or diametral pitch).

mechanismChecks.pass: An input gear, at least one compound shaft that carries two or more gears fixed together, an output gear, and shafts with supports. At least two meshes. Different gear sizes on the compound shaft are usual, not required.

The gears on the compound shaft turn as one. Each mesh is between gears on different parallel shafts and meshes correctly. Pitch-circle tangency is judged only if pitch circles are shown or dimensioned.
Meshed external gears turn in opposite directions. The two gears on the compound shaft turn in the same direction.

Stage speeds follow the actual tooth counts (a smaller driving gear turns a larger driven gear slower, and the reverse), and a stated overall ratio equals the product of the stage ratios in either convention (within 10 % where turns or teeth are resolved). Not every stage must reduce speed.
No unintended solid intersection: shafts may pass through gear bores, and teeth in mesh may touch. No gear floats without a shaft. Meshed gears have the same tooth size.

questions.question: Why do helical gears run more quietly than straight-cut gears, and why do they push sideways on their shafts?
questions.teachingValue: Connects tooth shape to noise and to bearing loads; a standard design trade-off.

keyFacts.fact: Helical gear teeth are cut at an angle (the helix angle) to the gear axis; straight-cut (spur) teeth are parallel to the axis.

Compared with otherwise comparable spur gears, helical gears engage more gradually and have an added overlap contact ratio (more teeth share the load), which often reduces vibration and noise. Noise also depends on accuracy, load, speed and the gearbox.
Two externally meshed helical gears on parallel shafts have opposite hands (one left-hand, one right-hand) and equal helix angles. An internal helical gear and its pinion have the same hand.

The tooth force has a component along the shaft axis (axial thrust): Wa = Wt x tan(helix angle). The bearings must carry this thrust. It grows with the helix angle. The thrusts on the two meshed gears are equal and opposite.
In a symmetric, equally loaded double-helical (herringbone) gear, the opposite helices cancel the resultant axial thrust; unequal loading can leave some residual thrust.

mechanismChecks.pass: Two meshed gears with visibly slanted teeth, their shafts, and bearings or supports. A spur gear for comparison is allowed but not required.
The shafts are parallel and the gears mesh. An external pair has opposite hands, so the slanted teeth match at the mesh; an internal pair has the same hand.
An external pair turns in opposite directions; an internal pair turns in the same direction.

Relative speeds follow the tooth counts where they are resolved. If thrust arrows are drawn, they act along the shaft axes, are opposite on the two gears, and their sense agrees with the helix hand, the rotation and which gear drives. If no thrust arrows are drawn, the thrust part is NOT SHOWN.
Teeth do not pass through each other; the slant of the teeth stays continuous across the face.

questions.question: Why does a planetary gear set turn backward when you hold the planet carrier still?
questions.teachingValue: Teaches that the held member decides the behaviour of an epicyclic set and that internal and external meshes differ in direction.

keyFacts.fact: A planetary set has a central sun gear, planet gears on a carrier, and a ring gear with internal teeth. Each planet meshes with both the sun and the ring.
With the carrier held, the planet axles cannot move, so the planets spin in place like idler gears.
The sun-to-planet mesh is external and reverses direction; the planet-to-ring mesh is internal and keeps direction. So the ring turns opposite to the sun.
With the carrier held: ring speed / sun speed = -(sun teeth / ring teeth). Example: sun 24, ring 60: the ring turns at 0.4 x sun speed, backward. The planet tooth count does not change this ratio.
For standard gears, ring teeth = sun teeth + 2 x planet teeth; with equally spaced planets, (sun teeth + ring teeth) must be divisible by the number of planets.

mechanismChecks.pass: A sun gear, at least one planet gear, a carrier and a ring gear with internal teeth. Two or more planets are common, not required.
Each planet sits on a carrier pin and meshes with both the sun and the ring. The carrier is shown held (fixed to the frame or marked as held).
The carrier does not move. The planets spin about their own pins. The ring turns opposite to the sun.
The ring turns slower than the sun, at sun teeth / ring teeth of the sun speed (within 10 % where it can be judged). A stated ratio matches the stated or visible tooth counts.

The planets touch both the sun and the ring without overlap or gap. For standard gears with one module, ring teeth = sun teeth + 2 x planet teeth, judged only when tooth counts are resolved or stated; visible planets are evenly spaced. No gear passes through another part.

questions.nearShipped: Examples/Solid3D planetary.json and planetary-components.json (ring held, sun in, carrier out) and docs/assets/from-a-prompt/robot-joint (two stages, ring held). This question holds the carrier instead; the ring-held reduction question is excluded. Marty's prompts may contain a planetary worked example: a known possible advantage for Arm 1.

questions.question: How does a worm gear make such a big speed reduction, and why do some worm gears lock so the gear cannot turn the worm back?
questions.teachingValue: Large ratios in one stage, sliding contact and friction, and the limits of self-locking (a common misconception).

keyFacts.fact: In the usual right-angle worm drive, a worm (a screw-like gear with one or more threads, called starts) meshes with a worm wheel on a perpendicular shaft that does not intersect the worm shaft. Other shaft angles are possible.
Each turn of the worm moves the wheel by as many teeth as the worm has starts. Ratio = wheel teeth / worm starts (example: 40 teeth, single start: 40:1).
The teeth mostly slide on each other, so friction losses are higher and efficiency is lower than for spur gears; efficiency falls as the lead angle gets smaller.

A worm drive is self-locking (the wheel cannot drive the worm) only when friction is large compared with the lead angle: about friction coefficient > cos(normal pressure angle) x tan(lead angle). Many worm drives are not self-locking.
Self-locking is not a reliable brake: vibration and lower running friction can let a drive back-drive.

mechanismChecks.pass: A worm with a helical thread, a worm wheel, and both shafts with supports.
The shafts are offset (they do not intersect); the usual drive is at right angles, and a correct worm drive at another shaft angle is accepted. The worm thread engages the wheel teeth.

The worm and the wheel each turn about their own axes. Where the worm's helix hand is visible, the wheel's sense of rotation follows the worm's hand and rotation; otherwise judge only that both turn about their own axes.

The wheel turns slower than the worm, at worm starts / wheel teeth of the worm speed (within 10 % where turns and teeth are resolved). The number of starts and self-locking are NOT SHOWN unless they are labelled. No minimum reduction is required.
For the usual right-angle pair, the worm's axial pitch matches the wheel's circular pitch where it is resolved; similar-looking spacing alone is not proof. No part passes through another.

questions.question: How does rack-and-pinion steering turn a car's front wheels when you turn the steering wheel?
questions.teachingValue: Rotation to straight-line motion, then linkages to a turning wheel; an everyday system.

keyFacts.fact: The steering wheel turns a shaft (the steering column) with a small pinion gear at its lower end.
The pinion meshes with a straight toothed bar, the rack, in a housing across the car. Turning the pinion slides the rack left or right.
For a constant-ratio rack and pinion, the rack moves pi x pinion pitch diameter for each turn of the pinion. A variable-ratio steering rack need not move the same distance for each turn.
Tie rods connect the ends of the rack to steering arms on the wheel hubs (knuckles); the wheels pivot about near-vertical steering axes.

In conventional low-speed Ackermann steering, both front wheels turn toward the side to which the steering wheel is turned, and the inner wheel turns more. Parallel and anti-Ackermann layouts also exist.
Many cars add hydraulic or electric power assist to the rack or column.

mechanismChecks.pass: Steering wheel and column, pinion, rack, tie rods, steering arms or knuckles, and two front wheels.
The pinion meshes with the rack. The tie rods join the rack ends to the steering arms with joints. Each wheel pivots about a steering axis.

From the driver's view: turning the steering wheel moves the rack sideways in the direction that the pinion placement (above or below the rack) gives, and the steering-arm geometry (arms in front of or behind the steering axes) turns both wheels toward the side to which the steering wheel is turned.

For a constant-ratio rack, rack travel is proportional to pinion rotation, and a stated travel per turn equals pi x pitch diameter; a correctly shown variable-ratio rack is accepted. The wheels steer through a limited angle, not a full turn.
The tie rods keep a constant length. The rack stays straight in its housing. No wheel passes through the body or another part.

questions.conventional: the mechanism as the key facts describe it

questions.question: How does a windshield wiper turn a spinning motor into a back-and-forth sweep?
questions.teachingValue: The crank-rocker four-bar linkage and the Grashof condition in a familiar machine.

keyFacts.fact: For the conventional crank-driven wiper: an electric motor turns a gear reduction (often a worm gear) whose output crank turns continuously, all the way around.
acceptedWordings: A stated reduction of another kind (not a worm gear) is not an error.
keyFacts.designerNote: The worm-gear detail is common practice, not a requirement.

keyFacts.fact: For the conventional crank-rocker: a connecting rod (coupler) joins the crank to a lever (rocker) on the wiper pivot shaft. The crank, rod, rocker and the fixed body form a four-bar linkage of the crank-rocker type.
For the conventional crank-rocker: as the crank makes one full turn, the rocker swings once back and forth through a fixed angle, and the wiper arm on the pivot shaft sweeps the glass.

For the conventional crank-rocker: the crank turns fully and reliably when the strict Grashof condition holds, shortest link + longest link < sum of the other two links, with the shortest link as the crank next to the fixed link. Equality is a change-point linkage that can lock or flip at its dead points. If the fixed link is the shortest, the linkage is a double-crank, in which both side links turn fully.
A second linkage can transmit the same drive to a second wiper; its connections and relative sweep depend on the layout.
keyFacts.designerNote: Sol labelled it single-source (PLAUSIBLE); the Gemini check gave a second independent source.

keyFacts.fact: For a reversing-motor drive: the motor (or its control) reverses at each end of the sweep, so the wiper swings back and forth without a continuously turning crank.

factCheck.action: added in key version 2 for an accepted variant (fact-check section C)

keyFacts.fact: For a rack drive: a crank-driven slider moves a toothed rack or a cable-rack back and forth, and the rack turns a pinion on each wiper spindle, so the spindle swings back and forth.

factCheck.action: added in key version 2 for an accepted variant (fact-check section C)

mechanismChecks.pass: Conventional crank-rocker: a motor (with or without a visible reduction), a crank, a connecting rod, a rocker on the wiper pivot, a wiper arm or blade, and fixed pivots. Accepted variant: its own drive parts (a reversing motor and its links; or a slider with a rack or cable-rack and pinions), the wiper arm or blade, and fixed pivots.
Crank-rocker: four links joined by four pivots in a closed loop, with the rocker fixed to the wiper pivot shaft. Accepted variant: the parts are joined as that drive needs.
The wiper swings back and forth and reverses at two end positions. Crank-rocker: the crank turns continuously in one direction. Reversing-motor drive: the motor output reverses at each end.
One full wipe cycle (out and back) per crank turn (crank-rocker) or per drive cycle (accepted variant). The sweep angle is the same in every cycle.

Every link keeps its length and every joint is feasible. The crank-rocker completes its turns without locking or flipping (no change-point behaviour unless it is explained). Links that cross in a 2-D projection are not a collision. The wiper does not pass through the glass.

questions.conventional: a crank-rocker four-bar linkage driven by a continuously turning crank

acceptedVariants.description: A reversing motor drives the wiper arm or arms directly or through links, with no continuously turning crank.
A crank-driven slider moves a toothed rack or a cable-rack that turns a pinion on each wiper spindle; or a sector gear drives a pinion.

questions.question: How does Watt's linkage make a point move in an almost straight line?
questions.teachingValue: Approximate straight-line motion from pure rotation; a historic steam-engine problem still used in car suspensions.

keyFacts.fact: A conventional Watt linkage has two rockers, each pivoted to the fixed frame at one end, on opposite sides, and joined at their moving ends by a short coupler.
keyFacts.designerNote: The FIRGELLI page was replaced: it does not establish the construction (Sol, SOURCE-MISMATCH).

keyFacts.fact: The free end of each rocker moves on an arc, and the two arcs curve in opposite directions. When the two rockers have equal length (the usual symmetric construction), their sideways movements approximately cancel near the middle of the motion at the midpoint of the coupler; for unequal rockers, the tracing point divides the coupler in inverse proportion to the rocker lengths. The cancellation is approximate and local, not exact.

For equal-length rockers, the midpoint of the coupler traces a figure-eight curve (Watt's curve) whose middle part is nearly straight; for unequal rockers, the point that divides the coupler in inverse proportion to the rocker lengths traces such a path. The line is approximate, not exact; the error grows with the stroke.
acceptedWordings: Calling the curve 'lemniscate-like' or 'figure-eight' is correct.
Calling the path exactly straight is an error.

keyFacts.fact: James Watt described the linkage in 1784 to guide a steam-engine piston rod in an approximately straight line; today it is also used to locate a car's rear axle sideways.
keyFacts.designerNote: The FIRGELLI page was replaced: it does not establish the date or the uses (Sol, SOURCE-MISMATCH).

mechanismChecks.pass: Two rockers, a coupler, two fixed pivots, and the traced point marked on the coupler.
Each rocker hinges to the frame at its outer end, the two pivots on opposite sides; the coupler hinges to both free ends.

The motion is consistent with the shown geometry: on the straight working branch the two rockers turn in opposite senses (on the outer loops of a full figure-eight they can turn in the same sense). A coupler tilt too small to see is not a failure.

The traced point follows an approximately straight path in its working segment. A full figure-eight and an exactly central tracing point are not required (unequal rockers move the best tracing point). No text or graphic calls the path exactly straight.
Every link keeps its length and the pivots stay fixed. Links that cross in projection or lie in separate planes are not a collision; only a true solid collision fails.

questions.question: How does a shaping machine's quick-return mechanism cut slowly and come back fast?
questions.teachingValue: A slider-crank inversion where a constant-speed crank gives unequal stroke times; time ratio from crank angles.

keyFacts.fact: A crank turning at constant speed carries a sliding block in the slot of a lever. The lever pivots at a fixed point and swings back and forth; a link from the lever drives the ram, which carries the cutting tool in a straight guide.
acceptedWordings: The Whitworth form (a crank and a rotating slotted link) is also correct if it is described correctly.
keyFacts.designerNote: The fact describes the crank-and-slotted-lever form.

keyFacts.fact: The cutting stroke happens over a larger crank angle than the return stroke. At constant crank speed, time ratio = cutting crank angle / return crank angle, which is more than 1.

In the crank-and-slotted-lever form (the lever pivot lies outside the crank-pin circle), the two end positions of the oscillating lever are where its slot centreline is tangent to the crank-pin circle; these split the crank turn into the two unequal angles. In the Whitworth form, the slotted link's pivot lies inside the crank-pin circle and the slotted link turns a full 360 degrees.
It is an inversion of the slider-crank chain.

mechanismChecks.pass: A crank, a sliding block, a slotted link with a fixed pivot, a link or direct drive to the ram, the ram with its tool, and the frame or guide, in the crank-and-slotted-lever form or the Whitworth form.

The connections of the shown form: the block turns on the crank pin and slides in the slot; the slotted link's pivot is fixed (outside the crank-pin circle for the crank-and-slotted-lever, inside it for Whitworth); the ram moves in a straight guide.

The crank turns in one direction. The slotted link swings (crank-and-slotted-lever) or rotates (Whitworth). The ram moves back and forth. The slow stroke is the cutting stroke only when a tool, a workpiece or a label makes the cutting direction judgeable; otherwise judge only that one stroke is slow and the return is fast.

At constant crank speed the cutting stroke visibly takes longer than the return stroke; measure complete strokes, not instantaneous ram speed. A stated time ratio is more than 1 and equals the ratio of the stated crank angles.
The block stays in the slot. Links keep their lengths. No part passes through another.

questions.nearShipped: Examples/Solid3D slider-crank.json and slider-crank-component.json (the plain slider-crank). That question is excluded; this is a different inversion with a different teaching point.
questions.conventional: the crank-and-slotted-lever quick-return mechanism

acceptedVariants.description: The Whitworth quick-return mechanism: the slotted link's pivot is inside the crank-pin circle and the slotted link turns a full 360 degrees.

questions.question: How does a camshaft open and close an engine's valves at the right time?
questions.teachingValue: Cam lobes, followers and springs, and the 2:1 timing drive of a four-stroke engine.

keyFacts.fact: The camshaft carries egg-shaped lobes (cams). As it turns, a lobe pushes a follower (tappet or lifter, sometimes through a pushrod and rocker arm), which pushes the valve open.
For the conventional spring-return valvetrain: the valve spring closes the valve and keeps the follower on the cam within the design speed range.
In a four-stroke engine the camshaft turns at half the crankshaft speed (a 2:1 belt, chain or gear drive), so each valve opens once every two crankshaft turns.

For a four-stroke engine with inward-opening poppet valves: the lobes are phased so the intake valve opens around the intake stroke and the exhaust valve around the exhaust stroke. Real valve events can start before or end after the stroke boundaries and can overlap. The valves open inward, into the cylinder.
On the round part of the cam (base circle) the valve is closed; the lift follows the lobe shape.
For a desmodromic valvetrain: a second cam lobe and a closing rocker close the valve positively; no spring is needed to close it.

factCheck.action: added in key version 2 for an accepted variant (fact-check section C)

keyFacts.fact: For a two-stroke engine with poppet valves: the camshaft turns at crankshaft speed (1:1), so each valve opens once per crankshaft turn.

factCheck.action: added in key version 2 for an accepted variant (fact-check section C)

mechanismChecks.pass: A camshaft with at least one lobe, a follower, a poppet valve and the cylinder head or port. Conventional: a valve spring. Desmodromic variant: a closing lobe and closing rocker instead of the spring.

The follower (or its roller) touches the lobe, directly or through the shown linkage. Conventional: the spring sits between the head and the valve retainer. If the crankshaft is shown, a drive links it to the camshaft.
The valve moves into the cylinder to open and back out to close; the follower and any linkage move as the shown geometry requires.

The valve opens once per camshaft turn and is closed on the base circle. If the crankshaft or the timing drive is shown: four-stroke, the crankshaft turns twice per camshaft turn (two-stroke variant: once). Valve events may lead, lag and overlap the stroke boundaries. If no crankshaft or timing drive is shown, the crank-timing part (and key fact K3) is NOT SHOWN.

No visibly impossible penetration. A hidden gap is not lost contact; a specified valve lash or a positive (desmodromic) closure is allowed. A spring, if shown, gets shorter when the valve opens. The valve does not pass through the piston.

questions.conventional: a four-stroke engine with a spring-return poppet-valve valvetrain and the camshaft at half crankshaft speed

acceptedVariants.description: A desmodromic valvetrain: a second cam lobe and a closing rocker close the valve, with no closing spring.
A two-stroke engine with poppet valves: the camshaft turns at crankshaft speed (1:1).

questions.question: How can a spinning cam make a follower rise, pause, and drop back once every turn?
questions.teachingValue: Profile radius to follower motion, dwell from a constant-radius arc, and how designers plan cam motion.

keyFacts.fact: A plate (disk) cam turns on a shaft. A follower (knife-edge, roller or flat-faced) rests on its edge and moves in a guide.

The follower position is set by the cam's lift along the follower's line of motion: for an in-line knife-edge follower, the distance from the cam axis to the contact point; for a roller follower, the distance along the guide to the roller centre on the pitch curve; for a flat-faced follower perpendicular to its motion, the distance from the cam axis to the flat face (the contact point shifts sideways by ds/dtheta). For an offset follower, the lift follows from the follower geometry. Where the lift grows, the follower rises; where it shrinks, the follower falls.
keyFacts.designerNote: WRONG in the Gemini check: the contact-point radius equals the lift only for an in-line knife-edge follower.

keyFacts.fact: A dwell (pause) happens where the profile is a circular arc centred on the cam axis (constant radius).
A spring or gravity (force closure) or a groove (form closure) keeps the follower on the cam.

The motion repeats once per cam turn. Designers plan it with a displacement diagram (follower position against cam angle) and use smooth curves, such as cycloidal motion, so velocity and acceleration change without jumps.

mechanismChecks.pass: A cam on a shaft, a follower, its guide, and a spring, weight or groove that keeps contact.
The follower moves in its guide and touches the cam.
The cam turns in one direction. The follower moves up and down along its guide only.

At least one rise, one dwell and one return per cam turn; a double dwell and a dwell at any position are allowed. Each dwell happens while a constant-radius arc centred on the cam axis is under the follower.

The contact follows the actual follower type (knife-edge, roller, flat-faced or offset). The follower neither passes into the cam nor leaves it, unless the text explains why; normal clearance in a form-closed groove is not lost contact.

questions.question: How does a Geneva drive turn steady rotation into stop-and-go steps?
questions.teachingValue: Intermittent motion with positive locking, used in film projectors and indexing tables.

keyFacts.fact: The driver wheel carries a pin on an arm and a raised locking disc. The driven wheel has n radial slots with concave arcs between them.
For each driver turn, the pin enters a slot, turns the driven wheel by one step of 360/n degrees, and leaves the slot.

Ideally the pin enters and leaves along the slot's length (the slot is tangent to the pin circle at entry), so the driven wheel starts and stops with zero angular velocity. The acceleration still changes abruptly, and clearance or flexibility can cause shock; tangency does not guarantee a knock-free drive.
While the pin is out of the slots, the convex locking disc sits in a concave arc of the driven wheel and holds it still (dwell).

For an external Geneva with n slots, the wheel moves during (180 - 360/n) degrees of the driver turn and dwells for the rest; with 4 slots: 90 degrees of motion and 270 degrees of dwell. The driven wheel turns opposite to the driver.

mechanismChecks.pass: A driver with a pin and a locking disc, a slotted driven wheel, and two fixed axes.
The pin engages the slots. The locking disc fits the concave arcs. The centre distance lets the pin reach into each slot.
The driver turns continuously in one direction. During each step the driven wheel turns in the opposite direction, then stops.
One step of 360/n degrees per driver turn. For n >= 4 the dwell is longer than the motion (n = 4: motion 1/4 of the driver turn).
The pin does not pass through wheel material. The locking surfaces do not overlap. The driven wheel does not move during a dwell.

questions.conventional: the mechanism as the key facts describe it

questions.question: Why does a car need a differential to go around a corner?
questions.teachingValue: Kinematic need for unequal wheel speeds and how bevel gears share one input between two outputs.

keyFacts.fact: In a turn the outer wheel travels a longer path than the inner wheel in the same time, so it must turn faster.

If both driven wheels were forced to turn at the same speed (locked axle shafts or a locked differential), a tyre would have to slip or scrub in an ordinary turn. A solid axle housing can still contain a differential.
The drive pinion turns a ring (crown) gear bolted to the differential case. Inside the case, spider (pinion) gears on a cross-shaft mesh with two side gears, one on each axle shaft.

When the two axle shafts turn at equal speed (normally straight running with equal effective tyre radii and no unequal slip), the case, spider gears and side gears turn together as one unit; the spider gears do not spin on their shaft.
In a turn, the spider gears spin on their shaft so one side gear speeds up as much as the other slows down. The case (ring gear) speed is the average of the two wheel speeds.
An open differential gives about equal torque to both wheels.

mechanismChecks.pass: A drive pinion, a ring gear, a case, at least one spider gear (two is typical), two side gears, two axle shafts and the wheels.
The ring gear is fixed to the case. The spider gears are on a shaft in the case and mesh with both side gears. Each side gear drives one axle.

The cornering state is shown: the spider gears spin on their shaft and the outer axle turns faster. If an equal-speed state (straight running) is also shown, the parts in the case turn together and the spider gears do not spin on their shaft; both states are not required. The final-drive pinion axis may be at right angles (bevel), offset (hypoid) or parallel (front-wheel-drive helical or spur final drive).
The case speed equals the average of the two axle speeds (stated values are consistent; visible speeds do not contradict it).
The differential's internal bevel gears mesh with correct geometry (their axes meet). The final drive may be bevel, hypoid (offset pinion axis) or parallel-axis. No gear passes through another part.

questions.conventional: a bevel-gear open differential with a right-angle bevel ring-and-pinion final drive

acceptedVariants.description: A hypoid final drive: the pinion axis is offset from the ring-gear axis.
A front-wheel-drive helical or spur final drive with the pinion axis parallel to the ring-gear axis.

questions.question: Why does one wheel spin in mud while the other wheel stays still with an open differential?
questions.teachingValue: Equal-torque behaviour of an open differential and why traction aids exist; corrects the 'all power goes to the spinning wheel' half-truth.

keyFacts.fact: An open differential splits torque about equally between the two axles (internal friction aside).
The wheel in mud can push only with a small force before it slips, so its torque is small, and the wheel with grip gets the same small torque: too little to move the car.
The case speed is the average of the two wheel speeds, so if one wheel stays still, the other spins at twice the case (ring gear) speed.
The engine's power goes into spinning the slipping wheel, not into moving the car.
Limited-slip or locking differentials, or brake-based traction control that brakes the spinning wheel, send more torque to the wheel with grip.

mechanismChecks.pass: The differential parts (pinion, ring gear, case, spider gears, two side gears, axles) and two wheels, one on a low-grip surface.
As in a differential: ring gear fixed to the case; spider gears mesh with both side gears; each side gear drives one axle.
The slipping wheel's side gear spins, the other side gear is still, and the spider gears spin on their shaft as the case turns.
With one wheel still, the other turns at twice the case speed. Equal torque on both axles is judged only from visible labels, arrows with values or a diagram, not from wheel speed.
The differential's internal bevel gears mesh with correct geometry (their axes meet). The final drive may be bevel, hypoid (offset pinion axis) or parallel-axis. No gear passes through another part.

questions.conventional: a bevel-gear open differential with a right-angle bevel ring-and-pinion final drive

acceptedVariants.description: A hypoid final drive: the pinion axis is offset from the ring-gear axis.
A front-wheel-drive helical or spur final drive with the pinion axis parallel to the ring-gear axis.

questions.question: How does a four-stroke car engine turn burning fuel into turning motion?
questions.teachingValue: The core thermodynamic cycle in mechanical form: valves, piston, connecting rod and crankshaft.

keyFacts.fact: Intake: the piston moves down with the intake valve open and draws in air (with fuel in many petrol engines).

Compression: both valves are closed and the piston moves up, compressing the charge. In the ideal cycle this is the whole upward stroke; in a real engine compression begins when the intake valve closes, which can be after bottom dead centre.

Power: near the end of compression the charge is ignited, by the spark plug in a spark-ignition engine or by the heat of compression in a diesel; the hot gas pushes the piston down with the valves closed. In a real engine the exhaust valve can open before bottom dead centre.
Exhaust: the exhaust valve is open and the piston moves up, pushing the burned gas out.

One cycle is four strokes and two crankshaft turns (720 degrees); each cylinder makes one power stroke every two turns. The connecting rod and crankshaft turn the piston's back-and-forth motion into rotation.

mechanismChecks.pass: A cylinder, a piston, a connecting rod, a crankshaft, intake and exhaust valves, and a spark plug (or injector for a diesel).
The connecting rod joins the piston pin to the crank pin. The piston is in the cylinder. The valves are in the head.

Piston direction and valve states follow the ideal stroke phases (intake down, intake valve open; compression up, both closed; power down, both closed; exhaust up, exhaust valve open); realistic valve overlap and lead or lag are accepted. The crankshaft turns in one direction.
Four strokes take two crankshaft turns. Ignition happens near the end of compression, not necessarily exactly at top dead centre.
The piston stays in the cylinder and does not hit the valves. The connecting rod keeps its length.

questions.conventional: the mechanism as the key facts describe it

questions.question: Why does a single-cylinder engine need a heavy flywheel?
questions.teachingValue: Torque fluctuation and stored kinetic energy; the difference between smoothing and adding power.

keyFacts.fact: A single-cylinder four-stroke engine makes one power stroke every two crankshaft turns; during the other three strokes the crankshaft must keep turning, and compression takes work.
So the engine's torque rises and falls strongly over each cycle, which would make the speed rise and fall.

A flywheel stores kinetic energy (1/2 x I x omega^2). It speeds up while the net shaft torque (engine torque minus load) is positive and slows down while it is negative. The speed need not rise throughout the power stroke or fall throughout every other stroke.

Speed fluctuation (omega max - omega min) / omega average is about energy swing / (I x omega average^2): more inertia or a higher speed gives a smoother speed. Mass far from the axis adds the most inertia.

A flywheel generates no net energy or power: it alternately absorbs and gives back mechanical energy, smoothing the cyclic speed variation. More evenly spaced power strokes (more cylinders) can reduce the inertia needed, for comparable engines and loads.

mechanismChecks.pass: A cylinder, a piston, a connecting rod, a crankshaft and a flywheel.
The flywheel is fixed to the crankshaft. The connecting rod joins the piston and the crank pin.
The crankshaft and flywheel turn in one direction throughout the cycle.

One power stroke per two crankshaft turns. If a speed or energy trace or readable values are shown, the speed rises while net torque (engine minus load) is positive and falls while it is negative. Without a trace or readable values, the speed fluctuation is NOT SHOWN (it is too small to see).
The piston stays in the cylinder. The connecting rod keeps its length. The flywheel does not pass through other parts.

questions.conventional: the mechanism as the key facts describe it

questions.question: How does a Pelton water wheel turn a fast jet of water into spinning power?
questions.teachingValue: Impulse turbines: momentum change, split buckets, and the half-jet-speed optimum.

keyFacts.fact: In a Pelton (impulse) turbine, a nozzle converts the available head into a high-speed free jet at about atmospheric pressure.
keyFacts.designerNote: Cited to NPTEL Lecture 26, not Lecture 27 (Sol, SOURCE-MISMATCH).

keyFacts.fact: Pelton buckets have two cup-like halves separated by a splitter ridge that divides the jet into two streams.
keyFacts.designerNote: Cited to NPTEL Lecture 26, not Lecture 27 (Sol, SOURCE-MISMATCH).

keyFacts.fact: Each bucket turns the water through about 160 to 170 degrees relative to the moving bucket (about 165 degrees, short of 180 so the water clears the next bucket); the change in the water's momentum pushes the bucket. In the stationary frame, the leaving water's velocity is its relative velocity plus the bucket's velocity, so near the best speed it leaves slowly and nearly sideways, not necessarily backward.
In the ideal case the most power is taken when the bucket speed is half the jet speed; the water then leaves with little speed and falls away. Real wheels peak a little below half.
Pelton wheels suit sites with a high head and lower flow.

mechanismChecks.pass: A nozzle, the jet, a wheel with double buckets and splitters, and a shaft.
The jet is aimed along a tangent to the bucket circle. The buckets are fixed to the rim.

The wheel turns in the direction the jet pushes the buckets. Relative to the bucket, the water leaves both halves turned back (about 165 degrees); in the stationary frame, near the best speed it may leave slowly and nearly sideways. Both pictures are accepted.

Half the jet speed is the ideal best speed, not a required operating point. If speeds are stated or shown, a bucket speed near half the jet speed goes with slow leaving water, and other stated operating points are consistent.
The jet is physically plausible from the nozzle (it may curve slightly under gravity or spread). Water does not pass through bucket walls.

questions.conventional: the mechanism as the key facts describe it

questions.question: In a jet engine, how does the turbine keep the compressor spinning?
questions.teachingValue: The self-sustaining gas-turbine core: one shaft, energy taken by the turbine, the rest left for the jet.

keyFacts.fact: The compressor at the front squeezes the air; in the combustor, fuel burns in this air at about constant pressure; the turbine is behind the combustor.
The hot, high-pressure gas expands through the turbine blades and turns the turbine.
The turbine and the compressor are on the same shaft (a spool), so the turbine drives the compressor. A starter spins the spool up first; after that the engine keeps itself running.

In a pure turbojet, the turbine takes the shaft work needed to drive the compressor and accessories, and the rest of the gas energy, after losses, speeds the gas out of the nozzle as the thrust jet. In a turbofan the low-pressure turbine also drives the fan and takes a large share of the gas energy; shaft-power engines extract more useful shaft work.

In multistage axial compressors and turbines, rows of rotating blades alternate with rows of fixed vanes (stators, or nozzle guide vanes in the turbine). A centrifugal compressor is also correct and has no alternating axial rows.

mechanismChecks.pass: An inlet, a compressor (axial blade rows or a centrifugal impeller), a combustor, a turbine, a shaft and a nozzle.
The compressor and the turbine are on one shaft. The combustor is between them.
The gas flows from front to back. Parts on the same spool turn together in the same direction; separate spools may turn at different speeds. Fixed vanes do not turn.

A compressor and the turbine on its spool turn at the same speed. A faster exhaust is required only for the stream that produces thrust (for a turbojet, the exhaust jet is faster than the incoming air).
The blades stay inside the casing. The flow does not pass through solid walls.

questions.nearShipped: Examples/Turbofan (two-spool high-bypass turbofan cutaway). The general 'How does a turbofan engine work?' question is excluded. Arm 1 may have seen turbine parts in its library: a known possible advantage for Arm 1.
questions.conventional: a single-spool turbojet with an axial compressor

acceptedVariants.description: A centrifugal compressor (no alternating axial blade rows).
Two or more spools: each turbine drives the compressor (or fan) on its own shaft, and the spools turn at different speeds.
A turbofan: the core works as described, and a low-pressure turbine also drives the fan.

questions.question: Why does a turbofan get most of its thrust from its big fan instead of the hot jet?
questions.teachingValue: Momentum thrust and propulsive efficiency: move a lot of air a little rather than a little air a lot.

keyFacts.fact: A large fan at the front pushes air; most of that air goes around the core through a bypass duct. Bypass ratio = bypass-stream mass flow / core-stream mass flow. High-bypass airliner engines have ratios of several to one or more; an example number must name the engine, its date and the operating condition.
acceptedWordings: Qualitative statements ('most of the air goes around the core', 'several times more air goes around than through') are correct.
A specific bypass ratio is correct when it is hedged or tied to a named engine; a grader who cannot check a specific number lists it as unsure, not as an error.
keyFacts.designerNote: The universal 4 to 13 acceptance window is removed (both checks).

keyFacts.fact: Neglecting fuel mass and pressure thrust, a separate-stream turbofan's thrust is F = m_core x (V_core - V0) + m_bypass x (V_bypass - V0). The same thrust can come from a lot of air sped up a little or from a little air sped up a lot. Pressure terms are added when a nozzle's exit pressure differs from ambient.

For an ideal single stream with matched pressure and negligible fuel mass, propulsive efficiency = 2 x V0 / (Vj + V0): a smaller velocity increment gives a higher propulsive efficiency for the same thrust. A real turbofan needs a two-stream energy balance, and fuel burn also depends on thermal efficiency, losses and installation.

The low-pressure turbine drives the fan through the low-pressure shaft. In a direct-drive turbofan the fan turns at the low-pressure spool speed; in a geared turbofan a reduction gearbox lets the fan turn more slowly than the low-pressure turbine.
In a high-bypass turbofan the bypass stream generally supplies most of the thrust; its share depends on the engine design and the operating condition.
acceptedWordings: 'The bypass stream gives most of the thrust' is the expected statement.

A specific percentage is correct when it is hedged or tied to a named engine and condition. A percentage given as true of every turbofan is listed as unsure, unless it is plainly false (for example less than half for a high-bypass engine).
keyFacts.designerNote: The 70 to 90 percent window and the take-off percentage are removed. The DTIC source could not be opened by the fact check; FAA Powerplant Handbook chapter 3 is the only inspected source (single-source).

mechanismChecks.pass: A fan, a bypass duct, a core (compressor, combustor, turbine), the low-pressure shaft, and the exhaust streams.
The fan is joined to the low-pressure turbine by the inner shaft, directly or through a reduction gearbox (geared turbofan). The bypass duct surrounds the core.
Both streams flow from front to back overall (local swirl is not reversed flow). The fan turns with the low-pressure turbine (slower, through the gearbox, in a geared turbofan).

A stated bypass ratio or stream speeds agree with the picture. Duct area, arrow width or particle count alone do not show a mass-flow ratio or an exit speed: without readable values or calibrated graphics, the quantitative part is NOT SHOWN.

Where two or more shafts are shown, they are concentric; if only one shaft is shown, the concentric-shaft part is NOT SHOWN. The flow does not pass through walls (a cutaway's removed wall is not a wall).

questions.nearShipped: Examples/Turbofan and docs/assets/turbofan (two-spool high-bypass turbofan cutaway). The general 'How does a turbofan engine work?' question is excluded; this question tests bypass and propulsive efficiency. Known possible advantage for Arm 1.
questions.conventional: a direct-drive two-spool high-bypass turbofan

acceptedVariants.description: A geared turbofan: a reduction gearbox lets the fan turn slower than the low-pressure turbine.

questions.question: How does a gear pump push oil out using two meshing gears?
questions.teachingValue: Positive displacement and the counter-intuitive flow path around the outside of the gears.

keyFacts.fact: For the conventional external gear pump: two meshing external gears turn in a close-fitting housing; one gear is driven and turns the other.
On the inlet side the teeth come out of mesh; the space between them opens and the lower pressure lets oil flow in.

For the conventional external gear pump: the oil is carried in the spaces between the teeth around the outside of each gear, between the teeth and the housing wall, not through the middle between the gears.
For the conventional external gear pump: on the outlet side the teeth mesh again and push the oil out; the meshing teeth seal against flow back to the inlet.

It is a positive-displacement pump: a fixed volume per turn, so flow is about proportional to speed and nearly independent of outlet pressure (less internal leakage). A relief valve protects the system from overpressure.

For an internal gear pump (gerotor or crescent): an inner gear drives an outer internal-toothed gear set off-centre in the housing, and both turn the same way; the spaces between the teeth open on the inlet side and close on the outlet side (in a crescent pump, a fixed crescent separates the two sides).

factCheck.action: added in key version 2 for an accepted variant (fact-check section C)

mechanismChecks.pass: Two gears, a housing, an inlet port, an outlet port and a drive shaft.
The gears mesh. The housing closely surrounds the gear tips. The ports are on opposite sides of the mesh.

External pump: the gears turn in opposite directions, so the teeth carry the fluid from the inlet side around the outside to the outlet side; the inlet is where the teeth come out of mesh. Internal gear pump: both gears turn the same way, and the inlet is where the tooth spaces open.

The fluid moves in the tooth spaces from the inlet side to the outlet side (around the outside in an external pump). 'Fixed volume per turn, more speed more flow' is NOT SHOWN unless the speed varies or values are labelled; moving arrows alone do not prove a volume flow.
No bulk fluid path through the meshed teeth; explained leakage, relief or lubrication passages are allowed. The teeth do not pass through each other.

questions.conventional: an external gear pump

acceptedVariants.description: An internal gear pump (gerotor or crescent): an inner gear drives an outer internal-toothed gear, both turning the same way.

questions.question: How does a hand pump lift water up from a well?
questions.teachingValue: Check valves, atmospheric pressure and the 10-metre suction limit.

keyFacts.fact: In the common single-acting valved-bucket suction hand pump, a valved piston (bucket) moves up and down in a cylinder, and a lower one-way inlet (foot) valve admits water from below.

Upstroke: the piston valve closes and the water above the piston rises toward the spout; the inlet valve opens when the pressure below it exceeds the cylinder pressure. In a shallow suction installation, atmospheric pressure on the well water pushes the water up through it.
Downstroke: the inlet (foot) valve closes and holds the water; the piston valve opens and water passes through the descending piston.

At standard sea-level pressure, p_atm / (rho x g) is about 10.3 m of water, neglecting vapour pressure and losses; the usable suction lift is lower (about 7 m) and depends on conditions. Lift is measured from the pumping water level to the pump cylinder, not the total well depth. Deeper pumping water levels need a submerged cylinder or another pump type.
acceptedWordings: A practical suction lift stated as about 6 to 8 m is not an error.
keyFacts.designerNote: The 10.3 m figure is computed from standard sea-level pressure. The practical figure matches a pump supplier guide seen on 2026-11-11 (not a citable public URL).

keyFacts.fact: In the usual long-handle arrangement, the handle is a lever that reduces the hand force by its mechanical advantage while the hand moves farther than the piston.

For a deep-well lift pump: the cylinder with its piston valve and foot valve sits below the pumping water level at the bottom of a drop pipe and is driven by a long rod from the handle; it lifts the water mechanically, so the atmospheric suction limit does not apply.

factCheck.action: added in key version 2 for an accepted variant (fact-check section C)

keyFacts.fact: For a force (plunger) pump: a plunger and a check valve in the delivery pipe push the water up to the outlet on the downstroke.

factCheck.action: added in key version 2 for an accepted variant (fact-check section C)

mechanismChecks.pass: Conventional valved-bucket suction pump: a handle, a pump rod, a piston with a valve, a cylinder, a foot valve, a suction pipe, a spout and the water. Accepted variant: its own parts (deep-well: a submerged cylinder with its valves and a long rod in a drop pipe; force pump: a plunger and a delivery check valve).
The rod joins the handle to the piston. The piston valve is in the piston; the foot valve is below it.

The valve sequence of the shown design. Valved-bucket pump: upstroke, piston valve closed, foot valve open, water rises; downstroke, foot valve closed, piston valve open. Force pump: the delivery valve opens on the downstroke. A submerged cylinder need not be described as atmospheric suction. The handle and piston move consistently with the shown lever pivot.

Valved-bucket suction pump: water is delivered on the upstroke (inertia or an air chamber can keep some flow on the downstroke), and a shown or stated suction lift, measured from the pumping water level to the cylinder, is not more than about 10 m. Force pump: delivery on the downstroke. Deep-well pump: no suction limit applies.
Valves open only in the flow direction. Water does not pass through a closed valve.

questions.conventional: a single-acting valved-bucket suction pump with the cylinder above the water

acceptedVariants.description: A deep-well lift pump: the cylinder with its piston valve and foot valve is submerged below the pumping water level, driven by a long rod.
A force (plunger) pump: a plunger and a delivery check valve push water to the outlet on the downstroke.
